newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Woolworths warms to Asia, but cool on profit.
newsitem.headline: Woolworths warms to Asia, but cool on profit.

text.p: Australia's second-largest retail group Woolworths Ltd said on Thursday fresh food exports to Asia and a move into petrol retailing bolstered growth prospects, but the company cooled investor hopes for a short-term profit rise.
Speaking after the company's annual meeting, Woolworths managing director, Reg Clairs said a fresh fruit and vegetables export business started last year was a big growth opportunity.
"The potential is absolutely enormous -- I would suggest that by the year 2000 we would want to be hopefully exporting somewhere around A$100 million ($79 million)," Clairs said.
Earlier, Woolworths chairman John Iliffe said Woolworths exported about A$6 million worth of fresh food to Asian countries during the year to June, 1996.
"In the current year we expect to more than double this as the momentum of that activity increases," he said.
Iliffe said the appetite displayed by Asian customers for high quality fresh fruit and vegetables encouraged this view.
Clairs told reporters Woolworths had achieved a high level of market saturation in Australia and was constantly looking for ways to add new business to its existing stores.
The main opportunity identified, Clairs said, was the establishment of petrol outlets at its new and existing stores.
"Our ambition is to increase the total turnover of each store by a minimum of one percent," he said.
Woolworths' test petrol outlet site at a store in the town of Dubbo in New South Wales had so far slightly exceeded the targeted one percent increase, Clairs said.
Woolworths aimed to have 200 petrol outlet sites by the year 2000 which would account for about two percent of Australia's petrol retail market, Clairs said.
Woolworths, which is majority Australian-owned, had sales of A$13.99 billion in 1995/96 (July/June) and flat net profit of A$233.6 million.

"For the remainder of this financial year, competition will continue to be quite intense and it would be unwise to expect any significant improvement in profitability from an improvement in operating margins," Iliffe told the annual meeting.
However Iliffe said trading results for October had shown better signs and Woolworths was hopeful a recent improvement in consumer confidence would be reflected in Christmas trading.

Iliffe said although much depended on the Christmas trading period, an expanded Woolworths expected a sales increase of eight to nine percent for the year to June 1997 with growth of about 4.5 percent on a "same store" or comparable basis.
The more cautious outlook from Woolworths came three months after the company's managing director, Reg Clairs confidently predicted earnings growth for the retailer in 1996/97.
Speaking to reporters after the annual meeting, Clairs would only say the company was hoping for a slight increase in profit in the 1996/97 financial year.
